story: Jianxin Ni is the last author, usually the person who leads the project, of a 2026 prospective study from several Chinese centres on everolimus for kidney angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis complex (GAO2026B). In TSC the brake on mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is missing, and everolimus puts part of that brake back. In 183 patients the drug shrank tumours by half or more in 44% at 3 months and 83% at 6 months. Tumours with little fat responded better than fat-rich ones, so a scan of tumour fat could help predict who benefits. A lower dose looked similar and caused fewer mouth ulcers, but only in an exploratory, non-randomised comparison. Tumours regrew after the drug was stopped.

PubMed lists about ten papers with Ni at the urology department of Xi'an People's Hospital since 2023. They include a 2026 study in cells and mice showing that the protein PEAK1 helps prostate cancer resist the chemotherapy drug docetaxel by pushing nearby immune cells, macrophages, into a tumour-helping state, and a 2025 rat study on salt, IL-17 and cholesterol. No personal institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on these papers.

story: Amany Ahmed is the senior (last) author of HAFEZ2026, a mouse study of psoriasis, the skin disease with thick, red, scaly patches. The team caused psoriasis-like skin disease in mice with imiquimod cream and then gave melittin, the main peptide in bee venom. Melittin reduced the severity of the skin disease by about 60 percent. In the treated skin the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway was turned down and autophagy, the cell's recycling system, was turned up. This is a mouse study at a high injected dose, so it shows a mechanism worth testing, not a treatment for people.

PubMed lists Ahmed at the Pharmacology and Toxicology Department of Helwan University's Faculty of Pharmacy on about 25 papers since 2020, usually as senior author. The studies follow a common plan: a disease is induced in rats or mice and a drug or plant compound is tested for protection. Examples include the diabetes drug lixisenatide in a rat model of stroke (2020), the weight-loss drug semaglutide in a rat model of osteoporosis after loss of the ovaries (2024), and the plant compound phloridzin against lung scarring caused by the cancer drug bleomycin (2026), where autophagy was again one of the processes measured.

story: Hypertrophic scars are thick, raised scars that form after burns or surgery when skin fibroblasts make too much collagen. story: Edward Brignole is a co-author of three structural papers in the Atlas from David Sabatini's lab, all made with cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In cryo-EM, purified proteins are frozen in a thin layer of ice and photographed thousands of times with an electron beam, and the images are combined into a 3D model. The method needs careful sample preparation and microscope work, which is where an EM specialist comes in.

The three papers solve key parts of how mTORC1 senses amino acids. SHE2018 gives the structure of GATOR1, the complex that switches the Rag GTPases off, alone and bound to the Rags, and shows how it does so. ROG2019 shows how Raptor, part of mTORC1, docks onto the Rag-Ragulator complex on the lysosome: one part of Raptor reads the state of RagA and a separate claw reads RagC, and only the right combination lets mTORC1 land. VAL2022 gives the structure of human GATOR2, a large cage-like complex built on an octagonal frame, and maps where the sensors Sestrin2 and CASTOR1 attach. How GATOR2 holds back GATOR1 is still not fully settled.

Brignole's PubMed record shows a long collaboration with Catherine Drennan's group at MIT, with fifteen joint papers up to 2023. The Atlas papers list the MIT Department of Biology and MIT.nano, the institute's shared imaging facility. No official profile page was found, so the exact current title is not given here.

story: Rozalyn Anderson was senior author of a 2017 Nature Communications paper (MAT2017) that resolved an apparent conflict between two of the longest experiments in aging research. One group at the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and one at the University of Wisconsin had followed rhesus monkeys on calorie restriction, eating less without malnutrition, for decades. Wisconsin had reported longer survival and the NIA had not. Analysing both studies side by side, the paper found consistent health benefits in both, and showed that the survival effect depended on study design and on what the control monkeys were fed.

Calorie restriction is the oldest known way to slow aging in animals, and lower mTORC1 activity is one of the routes through which it is thought to work. Monkeys are much closer to humans than mice are, so this comparison is among the strongest primate evidence that eating less improves health. It leaves open how large any lifespan gain would be.

Anderson worked on calorie restriction in yeast in David Sinclair's group at Harvard Medical School. In 2003 she was first author of papers in Nature and Science showing that the enzyme PNC1, which removes nicotinamide, is needed for calorie restriction to extend yeast lifespan, and that this effect does not depend on swings in the cell's NAD+ to NADH ratio. At the University of Wisconsin-Madison she is in the Division of Geriatrics of the Department of Medicine and the Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center of the Madison VA hospital. Her recent papers cover how calorie restriction remodels the mouse brain, how an acetyl-CoA transporter in the endoplasmic reticulum changes neuron metabolism, and sex differences in aging.

studies.title: Caloric restriction improves health and survival of rhesus monkeys

story: Some kidney tumours are driven by faults in one signalling chain: the genes FLCN, TSC1/TSC2 and MTOR, which control mTORC1, and the TFE family of transcription factors that sit downstream. These tumours can look like other kidney cancers under the microscope, and getting the diagnosis right matters for treatment and for spotting inherited syndromes such as Birt-Hogg-Dube and tuberous sclerosis complex. The 2026 study in Virchows Archiv, led by Q. Li with Yang Zong as senior author, tested GPR143, a protein that can be stained in tissue sections.

GPR143 staining was both sensitive and specific for renal tumours with FLCN/TSC/MTOR-TFE alterations, which makes it a practical addition to the tests pathologists already use. The study is based on human tumour samples and is a diagnostic tool, not a treatment.

Zong was at the Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine of the University of California Los Angeles, where a 2024 Modern Pathology paper as first author described the genetic diversity of embryonic-type neuroectodermal tumours arising from testicular germ cell tumours; that paper notes the move to the University of Wisconsin-Madison. In Madison Zong also co-authored a 2026 study on the CXCL13-CXCR5 signal that draws CD8 T cells into clear cell renal cell carcinoma. A lab or profile page could not be checked.

story: Helmut Fuchs is a co-author on two Atlas studies that relied on large-scale mouse phenotyping, the systematic measuring of many body functions in the same animals. EIS2016 showed that oral spermidine, a natural compound also found in food, lengthened the lives of mice, kept heart muscle from thickening and kept the heart able to relax normally between beats. The benefit disappeared in mice whose heart muscle cells lack the autophagy gene Atg5, so autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was needed for the effect. The paper also included a human diet survey linking spermidine intake to lower blood pressure and fewer heart problems, but that part is observational and cannot show cause. NEF2013 gave rapamycin, the drug that blocks mTOR, to young and old mice and measured a very wide panel of body functions. Rapamycin lengthened life but changed only a few of the classic signs of ageing, so a longer life did not mean that ageing slowed down across the whole body. Both are mouse studies.

Fuchs works at the Institute of Experimental Genetics and German Mouse Clinic in Neuherberg, near Munich, and appears together with Valerie Gailus-Durner and the institute director Martin Hrabě de Angelis on more than a hundred PubMed papers. The German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich tests mouse models in a standardised way across many organ systems; its recent papers cover heart size, movement, behaviour, metabolism and blood values. Recent examples are a 2026 analysis of heart weight in more than 25,000 mice from the International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium and a 2026 mouse model of a genetic movement disorder, KMT2B-related dystonia.

story: Alain Scaiola is first author of the Atlas study SCA2020, a detailed three-dimensional picture of human mTORC2 at 3.2 angstrom resolution, sharp enough to place most individual amino acids. The structure was made by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), which freezes purified protein complexes in thin ice and combines hundreds of thousands of electron microscope images into one 3D map. mTORC2 is one of the two mTOR complexes and, unlike mTORC1, it is not blocked directly by rapamycin. The map shows why: the tail end of the protein Rictor covers the site on mTOR where the rapamycin-FKBP12 pair would bind.

Scaiola is also a co-author of STU2018, the earlier and lower-resolution architecture of the mTORC2 core (mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8). Both papers came from a joint effort of the groups of Timm Maier at the University of Basel and Nenad Ban at ETH Zurich, and they give drug designers an accurate picture of the complex.

Scaiola's publication record from 2018 to 2026 is in Nenad Ban's group at the Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics of ETH Zurich. Most of the work is on the ribosome, the cell's protein-making machine: a 2018 first-author structure of a yeast ribosome subunit caught in the last steps of assembly, and later studies with the Deuerling lab in Konstanz on how the NAC complex guides enzymes that trim and tag new proteins as they leave the ribosome (Nature 2024; Nature Communications 2026). story: Penny Lovat is a co-author of two Atlas papers from Viktor Korolchuk's lab at Newcastle University on why ageing cells behave as they do. CAR2017 showed that in senescent human cells (cells that have permanently stopped dividing) mTORC1, the growth-control complex, stays switched on even when nutrients or growth factors are taken away. The fault lies upstream, in how the cells sense amino acids and growth signals, and the cells come to depend on this signal to survive. KEL2024 showed that healthy human cells constantly recycle damaged mitochondria (basal mitophagy), that this stops when cells become senescent, and that part of rapamycin's anti-ageing effect on cells needs mitophagy to be restored. Both studies were done in cultured human cells.

Lovat's own research centres on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, in skin cancer. PubMed lists her at Newcastle University on more than 50 papers on melanoma and autophagy. Her group found that the autophagy regulator AMBRA1 and the skin barrier protein loricrin are lost from the skin above melanomas that are more likely to spread. With collaborators in Rome she showed that the HPV virus breaks down AMBRA1 in throat cancers, which lowers autophagy and makes the tumour cells easier to kill with cisplatin (2020). A 2026 study tested AMBRA1 and loricrin staining to help pathologists tell high-grade moles from thin melanomas.

PubMed papers list Lovat both at Newcastle University's Translational and Clinical Research Institute and at AMLo Biosciences, the Newcastle company that brings the AMBRA1 and loricrin test to clinical use. Details of training and academic title could not be confirmed from an official page.

story: Robert Lindquist is a co-author on two cell-biology papers from David Sabatini's lab that changed how the field thinks about mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The 2007 paper (SAN2007) found PRAS40, a brake that sits inside mTORC1. When insulin is missing, PRAS40 holds the complex back. Insulin switches on the kinase Akt, Akt tags PRAS40 with a phosphate, and the brake lets go. This helped explain how a hormone sets how strongly mTORC1 works.

The 2008 paper (SAN2008) answered a different question: how does mTORC1 know that amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, are available? The answer was the Rag GTPases, small switch proteins that bind raptor, part of mTORC1. When amino acids are present, the Rags bring mTORC1 to the place in the cell where its activator Rheb sits. Both findings come from experiments in cultured cells.

Lindquist's own line of work in the lab was screening technology. He is first author of a 2011 Genome Research paper that knocked down genes one by one in fruit-fly cells grown on printed microarrays and read the effect on TORC1-S6K signaling by microscope, which found new regulators of the pathway. He was also a co-author of the 2006 Genome Biology paper describing CellProfiler, open-source software that measures cell features in microscope images, and of the 2008 follow-up CellProfiler Analyst. PubMed lists him at the Whitehead Institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts. A current position could not be confirmed from an official source.

story: Shinzaburo Noguchi is a co-author of the two BOLERO-2 papers in the Atlas. BOLERO-2 was a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that had progressed on an aromatase inhibitor. Resistance to hormone therapy in these tumours is linked to overactive mTOR signalling. All women received the hormone drug exemestane, and half also took everolimus, an mTORC1 inhibitor related to rapamycin.

BAS2012, in the New England Journal of Medicine, showed that everolimus more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again, from 4.1 to 10.6 months by central review, which led to approval of the combination. Mouth sores (stomatitis) were the main side effect. PIC2014, in Annals of Oncology, gave the final overall survival: 31.0 months with everolimus and 26.6 months with placebo, a difference that was not statistically significant. The trial showed that blocking mTOR can slow a common cancer, but did not prove that it extends life.

PubMed lists well over a hundred breast cancer papers under this name from the Department of Breast and Endocrine Surgery at Osaka University, up to 2023. No official profile was opened, so the current title is not given here.

story: Cassidy Pumper is a co-author of two linked mouse studies from Dudley Lamming's lab in this Atlas (ARR2015, ARR2016). Rapamycin is the best-tested drug for extending lifespan in mice, but given every day it causes side effects such as poor blood sugar control and weaker immune responses. In ARR2015, mice given rapamycin daily (2 mg/kg) became glucose intolerant and their insulin-producing islets released less insulin. The same dose given once every five days left glucose and insulin tolerance normal, while dosing every three days was already too frequent. In ARR2016, female mice that started the every-five-days schedule at 20 months of age, which is old for a mouse, lived longer than untreated females. Taken together, the two mouse studies suggest that rapamycin's lifespan benefit can be partly separated from its side effects by giving it intermittently. This conclusion comes from combining two experiments in mice, not from a single study, and has not been tested this way in people.

PubMed lists three papers with Pumper's name, all from Lamming's group: the two Atlas studies and a 2020 eLife paper. That study found that removing the ovaries of female mice separates lifespan from metabolic health, and that the effect of losing mTORC2 in the liver depends on sex hormones. No later position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

story: Adam Waickman appears in this Atlas on two papers from Jonathan Powell's laboratory at Johns Hopkins that split T cell decisions between the two mTOR complexes. The 2011 Nature Immunology paper showed that mTORC1 and mTORC2 steer helper (CD4) T cells into different lineages. The 2015 Journal of Clinical Investigation paper did the same for killer (CD8) T cells: constant mTORC1 activity, after deleting Tsc2, produced aggressive but short-lived effector cells with no memory, while removing mTORC1 activity by deleting Rheb gave memory-like cells that still responded poorly to a second encounter with the antigen.

In the same period Waickman co-authored a 2015 PLoS One study from the lab showing that, within one batch of freshly activated CD4 T cells, the larger cells with high mTOR activity become glycolytic effector cells, while the smaller cells with low mTOR activity tend to become long-lived cells and regulatory T cells, a pattern also seen in human T cells.

story: Muscles grow when they are stretched and loaded, and mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is one of the main switches that turns that signal into new protein. Older muscle often responds less, a problem called anabolic resistance. Jonas Boritz Kristiansen is first author of a 2026 study from Kristian Vissing's exercise biology group at Aarhus University that tested which part of the signal is lost (KRISTIANSEN2026). Muscles from adult and old female mice were stretched in a dish. mTORC1 signalling switched on just as strongly in old muscle as in young, but a second stress pathway, JNK-SMAD2L, responded less with age. So, at least in this mouse model, the mTORC1 sensor for stretch seems to stay intact with age.

Kristiansen's other papers fit the same theme. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, as first author, pooled 46 human studies and found that older adults make muscle protein slightly more slowly than young adults at rest and after a meal, but respond about as well to exercise. A 2025 rat study, with the same group, looked at how weeks of voluntary wheel running affect oxidative stress and DNA repair in the brain. No institutional profile was found, so career stage is not given.

studies.title: Aging preserves mTORC1 but attenuates JNK-SMAD2L signaling sensitivity to passive stretch-induced tension development in isolated mouse skeletal muscle.

current.role: Researcher in John Kopchick's group at Ohio University who studies how switching off growth hormone action, even in middle age, lengthens life in mice
current.sub: Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging, Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine, Ohio University (papers 2025–2026) · Edison Biotechnology Institute, Ohio University (papers from 2019)
story: Silvana Duran-Ortiz is first author of an Atlas study (DUR2026) that asked whether blocking growth hormone still helps if you wait until middle age. Mice born without the growth hormone receptor are small, very insulin sensitive and the longest-lived laboratory mice known, but that may be because they never grew normally. Here the team deleted the receptor at 12 months, when the mice were adults. Both sexes still lived significantly longer, without big changes in body size. Males also kept better insulin sensitivity, muscle performance and bone structure as they aged, and the liver showed sex-specific changes in gene activity.

Growth hormone, insulin-like growth factor 1 and mTOR are linked growth signals, so the result fits the wider idea that turning growth signals down in adult life can slow ageing. It is a mouse study; in people, growth hormone receptor defects cause Laron syndrome, which is not the same as switching the receptor off in midlife.

Duran-Ortiz has published with the Ohio University growth hormone group of John Kopchick, Edward List and Darlene Berryman since at least 2019, first listed at the Edison Biotechnology Institute and more recently at the Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging. The work uses mice in which the growth hormone receptor is removed from the whole body or from single tissues such as fat, liver or muscle, and asks how each affects metabolism, immunity and lifespan; a 2026 paper found that old female mice without the receptor kept younger-looking B and T cell populations. No personal profile page was found, so the job title is not confirmed.

story: Ge Yang is the first author of YANG2026, which exposed young mice to polypropylene microplastics and the plastic softener DEHP. The mice developed changes resembling features of autism spectrum disorder. In their brains, mTOR was overactive and autophagy, the recycling process that keeps nerve cells healthy, was impaired. When the mice were given rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, autophagy recovered and the social and behavioural problems improved. Because the work is in mice, it points to a possible mechanism rather than a proven cause in children.

Yang has been first author of three papers from the same group. In 2023 the team showed that combined exposure to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP caused memory deficits and damage in the hippocampus of young mice. In 2025, in ACS Nano, Yang and colleagues showed that polystyrene nanoplastics upset the balance of proteins in the brain partly through changes in gut bacteria, and that the sugar trehalose could ease this damage.

story: Sarcopenia is the loss of muscle mass and strength with age. It makes falls and frailty more likely, and no drug is approved for it. In a 2026 review in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, with Helen Blau as senior author, Sara Ancel and colleagues survey the drug strategies now being tested. Among them are mTORC1 inhibitors, which may help because aging muscle has too little autophagy, the cell's clean-up system, and lowering mTORC1 activity can restore it. The review sets this against other approaches such as NAD-boosting molecules, urolithin A, myostatin blockers, drugs that mimic male hormones in muscle and blockers of the enzyme 15-PGDH. A review collects earlier work; it does not test these drugs itself.

Ancel trained in Lausanne, Switzerland, at Nestle Research and the School of Life Sciences of EPFL in Jerome Feige's group. There, Ancel was first author of a 2019 study showing that fat-forming progenitor cells in muscle help keep muscle stem cells young, and co-author of a 2019 Cell Stem Cell paper showing that aging disrupts muscle stem cells by reducing the protein WISP1 made by these neighbouring cells. In 2024, Ancel was first author of a study describing a two-colour reporter mouse for tracking different kinds of muscle stem cells in repair and aging.

Ancel co-authored a 2021 study from Helen Blau's lab at Stanford on heart muscle cells in muscular dystrophy, and now works at the Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases of Sanford Burnham Prebys in La Jolla. Ancel's exact position title could not be confirmed.

studies.title: Strengthening Muscle for Healthy Ageing: Innovative Treatments for Sarcopenia

story: Sepsis is a body-wide reaction to infection that can damage the brain, and survivors often have long-lasting problems with memory and thinking. In the Atlas study YU2026, Yu and colleagues used a mouse model of sepsis and looked at the medial prefrontal cortex, a brain region for planning and memory. mTOR was overactive there, and this stopped oligodendrocyte precursor cells from maturing into the cells that wrap nerve fibres in myelin, the insulation that speeds up signals. The mice lost myelin and did worse in a water maze memory test.

Breathing a high concentration of hydrogen gas lowered mTOR activity, restored oligodendrocyte maturation and myelin, and improved memory. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, had a similar protective effect, and a drug that switches mTOR on (NV-5138) was used to check the mechanism. For the Atlas, this is an example where too much mTOR activity is harmful in the brain. All of the work was done in mice.

Jiafeng Yu is listed in the Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital, and the Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology, in the group of Yang Yu and Yonghao Yu, which has studied hydrogen therapy in sepsis for several years. No other publication could be tied to this name with confidence.

studies.title: High-concentration hydrogen mitigates cognitive impairment in a murine model of Sepsis-associated encephalopathy by enhancing oligodendrocyte maturation and myelination in the mPFC

current.role: Muscle physiologist in the Rasmussen group in San Antonio who studies what overactive mTORC1 in skeletal muscle does to metabolism, inflammation and exercise adaptation

story: Erik Marchant is first author of the Atlas study MARCHANT2026, with B. B. Rasmussen as senior author. Overactive mTORC1, the growth-control complex, in muscle is often linked with insulin resistance, the state in which the body handles sugar poorly. To test whether one causes the other, the team switched mTORC1 on permanently in mouse skeletal muscle by removing GATOR1, a protein complex that normally turns mTORC1 off when amino acids are scarce.

The muscles showed more signs of inflammation, but the mice still handled a glucose load normally. So muscle mTORC1 overactivity alone was not enough to cause glucose intolerance, and other metabolic inputs must be needed. A companion paper from the same group in 2026, with Marchant as second author, found that this kind of hyperactive muscle mTORC1 blunted the benefits of endurance training even though mitochondria and lipids changed. Both studies are in mice.

Before San Antonio, Marchant published from the Department of Nutrition, Dietetics, and Food Science at Brigham Young University in Utah, including a 2020 study showing that, unlike a high-fat diet, bed rest did not appear to cause insulin resistance through mitochondrial oxidants, and a 2018 commentary on restricting branched-chain amino acids for metabolic health. In San Antonio Marchant has also co-authored human studies of muscle disuse and rehabilitation in middle-aged adults (2025) and of PDE-5 inhibitors (2026).

studies.title: Constitutive mTORC1 Activation in Skeletal Muscle Increases Inflammation but is not Sufficient to Impair Glucose Tolerance.

current.lab_name: Department of Integrative Neuroscience, Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies, Dartmouth College (Hanover, New Hampshire, USA)
current.role: Neuroscience researcher at Dartmouth who studies how growth signals shape the skeleton of sensory nerve fibres, and first author of work showing that PTEN acts on microtubules through mTORC2 rather than mTORC1
current.sub: Department of Integrative Neuroscience, Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies, Dartmouth College (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: PTEN is a brake on the PI3K growth pathway. When nerve cells lose PTEN, they grow larger and their axons, the long fibres that carry signals, extend faster. Both mTOR complexes sit downstream of PTEN: mTORC1, best known for driving protein synthesis, and mTORC2, which acts more on the cell's internal skeleton. In EVA2026, Simone Evans and colleagues at Dartmouth asked which of the two carries the signal in peripheral sensory neurons. Using mouse genetics, they removed PTEN together with either Raptor, an essential part of mTORC1, or Rictor, an essential part of mTORC1's sister complex mTORC2. Removing mTORC2, but not mTORC1, brought the fast growth of microtubules, the protein tracks inside axons, and the enlarged size of PTEN-deficient neurons back to normal. The effect was seen at the growth cone, the moving tip of the axon, not along the axon shaft. The work adds evidence on the less studied mTORC2 side of the pathway.

Evans is a member of the Department of Integrative Neuroscience at Dartmouth's Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies, the school that runs Dartmouth's PhD programmes. EVA2026 is the only PubMed paper found under this name and affiliation, so no wider research record is described here.

studies.title: PTEN regulates microtubule polymerization via mTORC2, but not mTORC1, in peripheral sensory neurons

current.lab_name: Department of Neurology, University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova (Craiova, Romania)
current.role: Neurology researcher in Craiova who works with Aurel Popa-Wagner on aging and stroke, and first author of a 2026 review on why mTOR-type lifespan gains shrink from worms to mammals
current.sub: Department of Neurology, University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova (2026) · Chair of Vascular Neurology, Dementia and Ageing, University Hospital Essen (2025 affiliation)
story: Blocking TOR, the yeast and worm version of mTOR, can lengthen the life of a roundworm several-fold, yet rapamycin extends mouse lifespan by a much smaller fraction. The 2026 review led by Denisa Pirscoveanu, with Aurel Popa-Wagner as senior author, asks why. It compares data from the worm C. elegans, the fruit fly and rodents and argues that in simple animals aging is steered by a few high-leverage pathways, while in mammals it is spread across many tissues with backup systems, feedback, hormones, gut microbes and the complications of getting a drug to the right place in the body.

The authors call this a shift from pathway leverage to system-level buffering. It is a synthesis of earlier results, not a new experiment, and it gives a framework for why a pathway like mTOR can matter a great deal in mammals while any single drug still has a limited effect on lifespan.

PubMed places Pirscoveanu in the Department of Neurology at the University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova in 2026 and, in 2025, at the Chair of Vascular Neurology, Dementia and Ageing of University Hospital Essen, University of Duisburg-Essen, where Popa-Wagner also works. Their joint papers since 2025 include work on immune genes and post-stroke damage in the aging rat brain.

studies.title: Biological limits of lifespan extension: evidence for a shift from pathway leverage to system-level buffering across species

current.role: Cancer researcher in Cherie-Ann Nathan's head and neck cancer group at LSU Health Shreveport, first author of a 2026 study showing that the mTOR inhibitor everolimus can turn immune-cold tumours hot in mice
current.sub: Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, LSU Health Shreveport (2024–2026, Nathan lab)
story: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma with a mutated TP53 gene often resists immunotherapy because the tumours are immune-cold: few killer T cells get inside. Priyatosh Nath's 2026 study, with Cherie-Ann Nathan as senior author, tested whether blocking mTOR could change that. A preprint version appeared on bioRxiv in June 2026 and the paper was then published in Neoplasia.

In mouse tumours of this type, including lines resistant to anti-PD-1 therapy, everolimus, an approved mTOR inhibitor, slowed tumour growth and remodelled the tumour surroundings. More CD8 T cells and dendritic cells came in, regulatory T cells that dampen immunity went down, and the HIF-1alpha/VEGFA signal that recruits immune-suppressing myeloid cells and builds blood vessels was reduced. Everolimus also raised the chemokine signals TNF-alpha and CXCL10 and lowered PD-1 and PD-L1, which helped T cells kill again. These are mouse results; the authors propose testing everolimus with immunotherapy in patients likely to fail immunotherapy alone.

PubMed lists Nath at the Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, LSU Health Shreveport, on papers since 2024, including a 2024 review on the growth-factor receptor FGFR2 in cutaneous squamous cell cancer with the same group and a 2025 review on the pharmacology of natural chalcones. The exact title could not be confirmed from an official page.

studies.title: mTOR inhibition augments antitumor immune effector response by reprogramming the TP53-mutant, immune-cold HNSCC tumor microenvironment

current.lab_name: Department of Urology, Institute of Urology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
current.role: Urology researcher at West China Hospital and first author of a study explaining how kidney cancers escape mTOR inhibitor drugs, and how blocking NEK7 restores their effect
current.sub: Department of Urology, Institute of Urology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (2026, at the time of the study)
story: Everolimus and temsirolimus, two drugs that block mTOR, are used for advanced clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most common kidney cancer. Many tumours stop responding to them. In the Atlas study TAN2026 in Nature Communications, Bo Tang was first author of work that traces one escape route. The protein SPOP attaches a K63-linked chain of ubiquitin, a small tag protein, to ZMYND8. The tag keeps ZMYND8 out of phase-separated droplets, small membrane-less compartments inside the nucleus. Freed ZMYND8 pairs with ZHX2 to switch on the gene for NEK7, and NEK7 activates p70S6K, a growth kinase normally downstream of mTOR, by a route that mTOR drugs cannot block. A PROTAC, a molecule built to make the cell destroy a chosen protein, aimed at NEK7 restored sensitivity to everolimus. The evidence comes from cells and animal models, not from patients.

PubMed lists Tang at the Department of Urology and Institute of Urology of West China Hospital, Sichuan University in Chengdu. Because the name is very common, no other paper was tied to this person with enough confidence to include, and no official profile page was found.

studies.title: SPOP-mediated ZMYND8 ubiquitination and phase separation exclusion drives mTOR inhibitor resistance in kidney cancer

story: Claire Goul was first author of a 2023 review in Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology (GOU2023) that explains how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, senses nutrients. mTORC1 is switched on at the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, when amino acids, glucose, cholesterol and growth signals are all present, and it then drives the making of proteins, fats and new cell parts. The review walks through the sensors and switches involved, including the Rag GTPases that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome, and how faults in this system contribute to metabolic disease, cancer and other conditions. It is a good entry point for a reader who wants the whole pathway in one place.

Goul's research in Roberto Zoncu's lab centres on the lysosome. In 2022 Goul co-wrote a short Developmental Cell commentary on lysosome repair, and in 2026 was first author of a Nature paper describing LASER, which links the sensing of lysosome damage to the assembly of the ESCRT machinery that patches the membrane. Goul also co-authored a 2025 EMBO Journal study showing that autophagosomes anchor a checkpoint that shapes PKA signalling in neurons.
PubMed lists Goul at the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at UC Berkeley on all papers from the Zoncu lab, 2022 to 2026.

studies.title: The molecular basis of nutrient sensing and signalling by mTORC1 in metabolism regulation and disease
